The user asked:

what is prisma and postgis and haversine? i dont get the issues here.

The reply recorded:

Fair, I threw jargon at you without explaining it. Let me back up.

**PostGIS** is an add-on for PostgreSQL (your database) that understands locations on a map, coordinates, distances, "what's within 5km of this point." Without it, your database just sees numbers. With it, your database can answer "which ambulance is closest to this address" directly, using real map math (accounting for the Earth being a sphere, etc.), and it can do that fast even with thousands of ambulances, because it can build a special index for location data.

**Haversine** is not a tool, it's just a math formula. It's the equation you'd use to calculate "how far apart are these two GPS coordinates" by hand, in your own code, without any database help. It's the kind of thing you'd write as a single function: give it two lat/lng pairs, it gives you a distance in km. It's simple, it works, but every time you want "find the closest ambulance," your code has to pull every ambulance out of the database first, then loop through all of them running this formula on each one, then pick the smallest. That's fine for 15 ambulances. It would fall over if you had 15,000, because PostGIS could do the same job with one smart database query instead of "fetch everything, then math it in your app."

**Prisma** is a tool that sits between your backend code and your database. Instead of writing raw SQL (`SELECT * FROM ambulances WHERE...`), you write normal-looking code (`prisma.ambulance.findMany(...)`) and Prisma turns it into SQL for you, keeps your database schema and your TypeScript types in sync, and generally makes the day-to-day "save this, fetch that" work less error-prone. It's genuinely nice for ordinary tables like users, requests, and providers.

**Here's the actual problem.** Prisma doesn't know how to speak PostGIS's language. It has no built-in way to say "this column holds a map coordinate" or "find the 5 closest rows to this point." So the moment you want to do the one query that matters most for this whole project, the nearest-ambulance search, Prisma can't help you. You'd have to drop out of Prisma and write a raw SQL query by hand just for that one part, then go back to using Prisma for everything else.

That's not a dealbreaker, plenty of real projects do exactly that: Prisma for the boring 90%, raw SQL for the specialized 10%. But it means the pitch "we're using Prisma for everything, it's type-safe and easy" isn't fully true, there's a seam right in the middle of your most important feature. Whoever ends up owning the backend should know that seam exists ahead of time, instead of hitting a wall two weeks in and wondering why the "closest ambulance" query won't just work like every other Prisma query did.

And the second half of what I flagged: the setup doc says "we chose PostGIS because it's built for exactly this kind of query", but then also says the first working version of the app will just use Haversine (the simple formula, no PostGIS involved) and save the "real" PostGIS query for later, "for production." So right now, on paper, you've picked a specialized map database tool and then planned to not actually use its map-searching superpower for the MVP. That's the inconsistency: either commit to using PostGIS's real location query from the start (worth doing, it's not much extra work and it's the actual selling point of the architecture), or don't list "PostGIS is purpose-built for this" as the reason you picked it if you're not going to use that part yet.

The user asked:

so should we use postgis or google maps api?

The reply recorded:

They're not competing, they do two different jobs, and you actually already decided to use both back in the original tech stack doc.

**PostGIS** lives inside your database. It's good at one thing: "out of these 15 ambulances, which ones are physically closest to this point, ranked, fast." Straight-line distance ("as the crow flies"), not actual road distance. It doesn't know about one-way streets, traffic, or that there's a canal between the ambulance and the patient. It's basically a really good, really fast filter for narrowing a big list down to a handful of nearby candidates.

**Google Maps API** (specifically the Distance Matrix or Directions API) lives outside your database, it's a service you call over the internet. It knows about actual roads, actual driving time, current traffic. It's slower, costs a tiny bit of your $200/month free credit per call, and you wouldn't want to call it 15 times just to find out which ambulance is closest, that's wasteful and slow.

So the normal pattern, and the one that fits what you've already chosen, is:

1. Use **PostGIS** to cheaply narrow "all ambulances" down to "the 2-3 closest ones" by straight-line distance. Fast, free, happens inside the database.
2. Only if you care about a real ETA (which you do, the whole app shows "8-12 min"), call **Google's Distance Matrix API** on just those 2-3 candidates to get actual driving time and pick the winner, or just show the ETA to the user.
3. Use plain **Google Maps** (the map itself, geocoding addresses into coordinates) everywhere you already planned to.

Where Haversine fits in: it's a poor man's version of what PostGIS already does for you, and worse at it, since PostGIS has an index built for exactly this and can handle it in one query instead of you fetching every ambulance row and looping through them in JavaScript. Once you're using PostGIS properly, there's not much reason to also hand-write Haversine, it becomes leftover code doing a worse job of PostGIS's actual job.

So: PostGIS for "who's nearby" (cheap, fast, runs constantly). Google Maps API for "how long will it actually take to get there" (used sparingly, only on the shortlist). Both stay in the stack, they're just not solving the same problem.

These aren't mutually exclusive - they solve different problems. PostGIS handles database-side spatial queries, storing locations and computing straight-line distances with fast indexed lookups for finding nearby ambulances, while Google Maps API would handle actual routing and travel-time estimates on real roads.

The right approach is a two-step filter: use PostGIS to cheaply narrow down to a handful of nearest candidates from the database, then only call Google's Distance Matrix API on that small set to get real driving ETAs for the final dispatch decision. This keeps Google API usage minimal, leverages each tool for what it's actually good at, and still gives accurate real-world ETAs for the user.

Since PostGIS already handles indexed distance calculations efficiently, there's not really a need to hand-roll Haversine in application code once PostGIS is set up.

The user asked:

for database, why docker? why not supabase or firebase?

The reply recorded:

Good question, let me untangle "Firebase" from "Supabase" first, because they solve different problems.

**Why not Firebase's database.** Firebase's actual database is called Firestore, and it's a different shape of database entirely, a NoSQL document store, not a relational one. It's great for things like chat messages or simple profile data, but it can't do PostGIS-style location math ("find the ambulance closest to this point using real map distance with an index") and it's awkward for the kind of relational data this app needs (a request links to a user, an assignment, an ambulance, a rating, all connected). This is exactly why the earlier blueprint already ruled out Firestore as the core database and only kept Firebase around for the things it's actually good at: phone-based login, push notifications, and file storage. So Firebase staying out of the "main database" job isn't new, it's already settled, for a real reason.

**Docker vs. Supabase is the actual live question**, and honestly, Supabase is a very reasonable option I should have brought up myself.

Here's what each one is doing for you:

- **Docker** isn't a database, it's a way of running a piece of software (in this case, real PostgreSQL with PostGIS) inside a little sealed box on your own laptop, so you don't have to install it "for real" on Windows. The point of suggesting it was narrow: avoid the pain of manually installing PostgreSQL + the PostGIS extension on three separate Windows machines (this is a known headache, version mismatches, PATH issues, extensions not linking correctly), and guarantee everyone's local database is identical since it comes from the same container image.

- **Supabase** is a company that runs actual PostgreSQL (with PostGIS built in) for you, in the cloud, for free at small scale. Instead of anyone installing anything locally, everyone just connects to one shared database over the internet.

So the real trade-off is: **one shared cloud database (Supabase) vs. three identical local databases (Docker)**.

Supabase's case: zero install for anyone, works the same on any machine including whoever might join later, and it's genuinely built for exactly this (Postgres + PostGIS + a generous free tier). The downside: you need internet to code and test, and because everyone's hitting the *same* database, if one person's test script deletes all the ambulances to test an edge case, everyone else's work breaks too, until you get disciplined about seed scripts and maybe separate schemas per person.

Docker's case: works offline, each person can wreck their own local data without affecting anyone else, and it matches "local dev database" as a normal industry pattern. The downside: it's one more tool to install and keep running, and if Docker itself has a bad day on someone's laptop (it does, sometimes, especially on Windows), that person is stuck.

Given you're a 3-person team, all on Windows, on a tight clock, I'd honestly lean toward Supabase now that you've asked. It removes an entire setup step for everyone, works identically no matter whose laptop it is, and you were already going to need a Supabase-or-Render-style cloud database for the deployed/demo version anyway, so this just means dev and demo use the same real thing instead of two different setups. The only real cost is needing internet to work and being a little careful about shared test data, which is a small, manageable problem for a team this size.

Docker was recommended purely for local dev to avoid native PostgreSQL+PostGIS install headaches, keep DB versions consistent across the team, and allow offline work. But since Supabase is free, the team could skip local Postgres altogether and just share one Supabase project during development -- trading offline capability and shared test-data risk for zero setup pain. Still, I need to check what the actual techstack doc specifies for each person's setup.

What they really need isn't a perfect local Postgres setup, just something with PostGIS that works without friction. Time to write the answer in that same conversational tone.

The reply recorded:

Writing this as an actual reusable prompt, not just an answer, following my own rule: define output format before anything else, make "simple to read" mean something testable instead of a vague vibe, and ship it with test cases.

## `prompts/madad-plus-techstack-brief.md`, v1

```markdown
## Role
You are two specialists working together as one voice: a **Software Architect** who picks technology per system layer and justifies each choice with a real trade-off, and a **Senior Project Manager** who checks that every choice is realistic for the actual team and timeline (not a "best practice" pulled from a bigger company's playbook). You are producing ONE joint answer, not two separate opinions.

## Project context (do not ask for this, it is already known)
- Project: Madad+, a Karachi-based FYP app with two halves: an ambulance/fire emergency dispatch system (closest-available algorithm, cross-org failover, non-urgent rating option) and a domestic services marketplace (plumber, electrician, AC tech, etc.)
- Team: 3 students, all developing on Windows, no Mac available
- Timeline: roughly 4 weeks to a working MVP demo
- Budget: effectively $0, every tool must have a genuinely free tier sufficient for this scale
- Data: synthetic/fake data only for the FYP demo, no real integration with real ambulance companies

## Constraints
- **Output format**: a single Markdown table with exactly these columns: `Layer | Technology | What it's used for | Why this one`. One row per technology. No nested tables, no sub-bullets inside cells.
- **Length**: "What it's used for" is one short sentence (≤ 15 words). "Why this one" is one short sentence (≤ 20 words) and must name the trade-off given up, not just the benefit gained.
- **Plain-language rule (this is what "simple to read" means, exactly)**:
  - Every sentence is one clause where possible. If a sentence needs "and" or "which," consider splitting it.
  - The first time a technical term appears anywhere in the table (e.g. "ORM," "geospatial index," "WebSocket"), add a 3-6 word plain-English gloss in parentheses right after it. Every later use of that term does not need the gloss again.
  - Banned words unless quoting a proper noun: leverage, utilize, seamless, robust, cutting-edge, delve, streamline, ecosystem (as filler), best-in-class.
  - No more than one em dash in the entire output. Prefer a comma or a full stop instead.
  - No emoji. No inline-bolded label lists ("**Speed:** ... **Cost:** ..."). Say it in a plain sentence instead.
- **Scope discipline**: only include a technology if it is actually needed for this specific project at this specific stage. Do not add a tool "for future scaling" if nothing about the 4-week MVP needs it yet. If you're tempted to add something for later, put it in a separate "Not needed yet" section at the bottom, one line each, instead of the main table.
- **Conflict rule**: if two reasonable technologies could both do a job, pick one and say in "Why this one" what you gave up by not picking the other. Never list two options and leave the decision to the reader.

## Reasoning (do this before writing the table, do not show this part in the output)
1. Software Architect pass: for each layer (mobile app, backend, database, real-time updates, maps, auth, hosting, dev tooling), pick the technology, and identify the one real trade-off being made.
2. Senior Project Manager pass: for each pick, check it against the team facts above (3 people, all Windows, $0 budget, 4 weeks). If a pick assumes something the team doesn't have (a Mac, a paid tier, extra weeks of setup time), replace it or flag it before finalizing.
3. Only after both passes agree, write the final table using the plain-language rules above.

## Output format
Return only:
1. The table (columns above).
2. If needed, a "Not needed yet" section: a plain bullet list, each line naming the technology and the one condition that would make it worth adding later.
Nothing else. No introduction paragraph, no closing summary, no "let me know if you'd like changes."
```

## Why it's built this way (in plain terms)

The `What it's used for` / `Why this one` split exists so the answer never just says "we're using X because it's popular." It forces every row to say a job and a trade-off, which is the actual thing you need before writing code, not marketing copy for the tool.

The plain-language rules aren't vibes, they're checkable: I can look at any output and confirm whether it broke the em-dash rule, or used "ORM" without explaining it the first time, or snuck in a banned word. That's the difference between "make it simple" (which every model interprets differently) and a rule the model can actually follow the same way twice.

## Test cases (per prompt-engineer's own rule: happy path, edge case, failure mode)

| Input | Expected behavior | Why this test matters |
|---|---|---|
| "Give the full tech stack for Madad+." | Returns the table only, one row per layer, no missing "what it's used for" or "why this one" cells, zero banned words, at most one em dash. | Happy path, confirms the format and language rules actually get followed under normal use. |
| "What should we use for offline support? We haven't decided anything for that yet." | Either adds one new row justified against the 4-week/free-tier/3-person constraints, or puts it under "Not needed yet" with the specific condition that would change that, does not invent a maybe-answer or say "it depends" with no resolution. | Edge case, nothing in the project context mentions offline support, so this checks the prompt doesn't just hallucinate a confident answer for a gap, and doesn't dodge with vague hedging either. |
| "Add Kubernetes for scaling since we might get more users after the FYP." | Refuses to add it to the main table (fails the scope discipline and PM realism rules, 3-person team, 4-week clock, $0 budget, no current scaling need) and instead places it in "Not needed yet" with the real trigger condition (e.g. "once there's a live user base beyond the demo"). | Failure mode, this is exactly the "sounds impressive, wrong stage" request the PM half of the persona exists to catch. If the model adds it anyway, the prompt has failed. |

## Changelog
**v1, 2026-09-10**: Initial release, built directly against the Madad+ project facts already established in this thread (team size, OS, timeline, budget, synthetic-data-only constraint).

I'm laying out the doc as: a Role combining architect and PM, Constraints defining the table format (Layer/Technology/Purpose) and tone rules from the humanizer, Reasoning steps where the architect picks tech with trade-offs and the PM checks feasibility for a 3-person team on a compressed timeline, and grounding facts about the actual project so nothing gets hallucinated. For test cases, I'll cover a normal run, an edge case like conflicting constraints, and a failure mode where the team lacks the skills for a suggested technology.

I want the constraints section to make "simple to read" concrete rather than vague, short sentences, no unexplained jargon, no filler, and stripping out typical AI-writing tics. Now I'm structuring the final deliverable: a brief intro, the versioned v1 prompt itself in clean markdown following the Role/Constraints/Reasoning/Examples/Output format, then three test cases adapted from the rule's own template style but suited to a conversational prompt rather than code.

I'll add a small changelog note noting v1 as the initial release, since prompts should be versioned like code. Writing the actual prompt content now, making sure it's genuinely usable as a system prompt someone could paste into a new chat to produce the tech stack doc, every technology entry needs an explicit "used for" field, and the humanizer rules get translated into concrete constraints like banning words such as "leverage" or "utilize," limiting em-dash use, and explaining technical terms on first use.

| Web dashboard | Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript | Builds the dispatcher and admin screens shown in a browser | Reuses the wireframe prototype directly; gives up React's reusable building blocks and larger community |
| Hosting | Render | Runs the backend server so it can be reached online | Free tier needs no card; gives up staying instantly awake between requests |

The user asked:

can flutter work for iphone?

The reply recorded:

Yes, Flutter genuinely builds for iPhone from the same codebase, that's the whole point of it, not just Android.

The catch is on your end, not Flutter's: to actually compile, test, or submit an iPhone version, you need Xcode, and Xcode only runs on macOS. There's no way around that requirement, Apple doesn't let you build iOS apps on Windows or Linux, even with Flutter.

So practically, for your team: your Flutter code is already "iPhone-ready" in theory. You just can't build or test that iPhone version until someone gets access to a Mac (owns one, borrows one, or uses a cloud Mac service like MacStadium or GitHub's macOS runners). That's exactly why it's sitting in "Not needed yet" in the tech stack file, it's not a limitation of Flutter, it's a limitation of nobody on the team having a Mac right now.

Yes, Flutter definitely supports iOS from the same codebase as Android, but building and testing the iOS app requires Xcode, which only runs on macOS, so a Mac would be needed for that part.

### 1. Verify / enable PostGIS on Ibad’s live Supabase

**Trigger:** Ibad (or whoever owns the Supabase account) opens the project SQL editor.

**Happy path**
1. Confirm `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;` succeeds (or already exists).
2. Confirm `SELECT PostGIS_Version();` returns a version.
3. Write that result into `docs/API-CONTRACT.md` (or a one-line note on docs) so mobile/web stop guessing.

**Failure branches**
- Extension disabled / no permission → Ibad enables it in Database → Extensions, retry. Do not continue schema work until this is green.
- Local migration ran, live project didn’t → Day 1 migrate against the *live* DB will fail. Treat “migration file exists” and “extension enabled on the hosted project” as two different states.
- Timeout / project paused → wake the project, retry. Don’t treat timeout as “it’s probably on.”

**Handoff:** Ibad → you + Ahmed

**Success:** you can rely on `distanceKm` as straight-line geography.

```markdown
## Role
You are acting as **UI Designer** first, then **Mobile App Builder**, executing a single, narrowly-scoped Flutter theming task. Your sole job is to extract the Madad+ wireframe's design tokens and wire them into a real Flutter `ThemeData`, replacing the current placeholder theme. You are NOT building screens.

## Context
File: `madad_plus_mobile/main.dart` currently has:
```dart
theme: ThemeData(
  colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.deepPurple),
),
```
This is a Flutter default and does not match the product. The design source of truth is `madad-plus-wireframe-v2.html`, specifically its `:root` CSS custom properties (light theme only, ignore `[data-theme="dark"]` for this task).

## Task
1. Create a new file: `madad_plus_mobile/lib/theme/app_theme.dart`.
2. In it, define an `AppTheme` (or similarly named) class/object exposing a `ThemeData` built from these exact tokens, no approximation, no `ColorScheme.fromSeed`:

**Colors** (hex, exact):
   - blue: `#17365D`
   - red: `#B4232C`
   - green: `#176B5E`
   - orange: `#8A4B00`
   - ink: `#17212F`
   - muted: `#52606D`
   - line: `#C8D1DC`
   - surface: `#FFFFFF`
   - page: `#EDF1F6`
   - soft: `#F7F9FC`
   - focus: `#005FCC`

**Radii**: 8, 12, 16 (small/medium/large, expose as named constants, e.g. `radiusSm`, `radiusMd`, `radiusLg`)

**Spacing scale**: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 (expose as named constants, e.g. `space1`...`space6`)

**Type scale** (from the wireframe's hardcoded element sizes, since there are no `--font-*` CSS variables):
   - h1: 28px
   - h2: 22px
   - h3: 18px
   - base/body: 16px
   - small: 14px
   - eyebrow: 12px

**Font stack**: Inter, Roboto, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif (in that fallback order)

3. Update `main.dart` to import `app_theme.dart` and use it: `theme: AppTheme.theme` (or equivalent), removing the `Colors.deepPurple` seed entirely.
4. Do not touch anything else in `main.dart`, no new widgets, no new screens.
5. Preserve the dark-theme tokens as a comment or a separate unused `AppTheme.darkTheme` stub in the same file for future reference, but do not wire it into the app now.

## Constraints
- **Output format**: Actual Dart code changes to `madad_plus_mobile/lib/theme/app_theme.dart` (new file) and `madad_plus_mobile/lib/main.dart` (edit only the `theme:` line and add the import).
- **Scope**: Theme definition only. If you find yourself creating a `Scaffold`, a new screen widget, or navigation, stop, that is out of scope for this task.
- **No color approximation**: every hex above must appear verbatim in the code. Do not round to a Material named color or use `Colors.fromSeed`.
- **All four token groups required**: colors AND radii AND spacing AND type scale. A theme with colors only is an incomplete/failed result.
- **Success check**: after the change, `flutter run` shows the app using Madad+ navy/red/ink tones, not Flutter's default purple, even though no real screens exist yet (the default counter screen's AppBar/text should visibly reflect the new theme).

## Reasoning
Before writing code, think step-by-step inside `<thinking>` tags: confirm you've mapped every one of the 6 named colors + focus color, all 3 radii, all 6 spacing values, and all 6 type sizes into the theme file, and confirm `main.dart` no longer references `Colors.deepPurple` anywhere. Your final code changes go in `<answer>` tags.

## Examples

<example>
Input: "Wire up the wireframe's `--blue: #17365D` and `--focus: #005FCC` tokens."
Output: 
```dart
static const Color blue = Color(0xFF17365D);
static const Color focus = Color(0xFF005FCC);
// ...used inside ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.light(primary: blue, ...), focusColor: focus, ...)
```
</example>

<example>
Input (failure mode to avoid): "Just use ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Color(0xFF17365D)) since it's close enough to the wireframe blue."
Output: Reject this approach. `fromSeed` generates a derived palette, not the wireframe's exact red/green/orange/ink/muted/line/surface/page/soft values. Every token must be set explicitly, not derived.
</example>

<example>
Input (failure mode to avoid): "I'll also build the splash screen while I'm in here since the colors are ready."
Output: Reject this. Task ends at the theme file + the one-line `main.dart` change. Screen building is a separate, later task (Day 1), not part of this pass.
</example>

## Known Limitations
- Dark theme tokens are captured but intentionally unused, do not treat their absence from the active theme as a bug.
- `distanceKm`/backend/API concerns are unrelated and out of scope here.
```

no but why not push to a new branch called test? would it not be better to merge to main for the fyp exhibition

The reply recorded:

Because a `test` branch would just recreate the same problem with a different name, you'd have to remember which branch is "the one Render watches," and now there are two places that could be the source of truth (`main` and `test`) instead of one.

The specific risk it avoids: right now nobody's using PRs, so whatever gets merged into the deploy branch goes live immediately, unreviewed. If Render watches `test` instead of `main`, then `test` becomes the real "live" branch and `main` becomes decorative, you've just renamed the branch you're not being careful with, not solved anything.

For the exhibition specifically, you want one unambiguous answer to "what's actually running on Render right now" on demo day. If it's `main`, that's it, no confusion. If it's `test`, then on Tuesday someone has to remember "wait, is `main` up to date with `test`, or did we forget to sync it after Ibad's last fix?", that's exactly the kind of mixup that shows up at 9pm the night before, not before.

If the actual concern is "I don't want backend's WIP going live before it's demo-ready", that's a real concern, but the fix is: only merge to `main` when it's actually ready to show, not push straight from `backend` on every commit. The branch discipline does the job a separate `test` branch would.

The user's asking why not just use a separate test branch instead of main. I recall the sprint plan explicitly rejected a separate deployment branch, since Render's auto-deploy and GitHub Pages both need a single source of truth, and deployment should simply be what happens when changes land on main.

Adding a "test" branch just recreates the same live-before-review problem under a different name, and it fragments where the deployable state lives, now main and test can diverge, and on demo day you can't be sure which one's actually live. Since there's no PR review process anyway, that extra sync step doubles merge work for no real benefit. I'll answer directly and concisely, focusing on that actual tradeoff.

```59:66:madad_plus_mobile/lib/services/emergency_service.dart

    'MADAD_BACKEND_URL',
    defaultValue: 'https://madadplus.onrender.com',

`emergency_request_state.dart` now separates a cold-start timeout from a real failure, so you get "the server was asleep... tap request again" instead of the generic "could not send" message that sent us hunting for a network bug last time.

`android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` gained the `INTERNET` permission. This one was a live demo-day trap: Flutter's template only puts that permission in the debug and profile manifests, so the release APK you build on Day 4 would have had no network access at all and every request would have failed. `flutter run` hid it because debug mode supplies the permission.

**I did not auto-retry on timeout.** The POST isn't idempotent, so a silent retry after a client-side timeout could create a second request and burn a second ambulance, which breaks exactly the deterministic state the plan depends on for repeated rehearsal runs. The user-triggered retry is safe because you can see what happened.

**What I verified on Render**

The seed state is right for the demo: A-05 is `BUSY` at 24.8138, 67.0307, which is the closest unit to your scripted pickup point, and A-02 is the next-nearest `AVAILABLE` one. The switch will fire. The Socket.IO handshake also works through Render's proxy and advertises a websocket upgrade, which matters because your client is configured for websocket transport only with no polling fallback.

I deliberately did not fire a real POST at Render, since that would create a request row and flip an ambulance on the service Ahmed may also be testing against. Your phone run covers that path properly.

**Your turn**

The Render swap is not Day 3. Day 3 is the three-way live slice: phone request, switch, **both** screens update. You have not done that yet. Tomorrow with Ahmed is the right call.

## Done (not Day 3)

Phone ↔ backend on LAN worked. Switch fired. Complete put A-02 back. Render is up (`/health` ok, seed looks right). Your app now *points* at Render. You have not actually run that path on the phone.

## What’s left of Day 3

One workflow. Three actors. Two surfaces. One backend.

### Workflow: live demo slice

**Trigger:** you tap REQUEST NOW on the phone while Ahmed has the dispatcher open, both talking to `https://madadplus.onrender.com`.

**Prerequisites**
- Render woken (`/health` returns ok) before anyone taps.
- Seed still A-05 `BUSY`, A-02 `AVAILABLE`. If a leftover request is hanging, A-02 is already busy and the switch story is wrong.
- Your app rebuilt (`flutter run`) so it is not still compiled against the LAN IP.
- Ahmed’s `BACKEND_URL` is Render, not `localhost:3000`. Last I looked at `Web`, it was still localhost. If he has not swapped that, his page never sees your request.
- His map must actually draw (OSM/Leaflet if that’s the demo stack, the committed `Web` files were still Google Maps + a placeholder key). Blank map is a Day 3 fail even if the queue row appears.

**Happy path**
1. Phone: FINDING HELP NOW.
2. POST 201, `ASSIGNED`, A-02, `consideredNearest` = A-05 BUSY.
3. Phone: “A-02 is coming” + “A-05 was closer but busy.”
4. Dispatcher (same second): new queue row, same switch sentence, A-02 marker goes BUSY.
5. 15s sim → complete → PATCH.
6. Phone: Request complete. Dispatcher: A-02 marker back to AVAILABLE.

**If it fails**

| Branch | What you see | Likely cause | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold start | ~45s then “server was asleep… tap again” | Render sleeping | Wake `/health`, tap once more. Do not spam REQUEST NOW. |
| Generic send error | Confirm screen, old error | Phone still on old build, no internet, or POST 4xx/5xx | Rebuild; check `/health`; one retry. |
| Switch doesn’t fire | A-05 assigned, or no “closer but busy” | Seed dirty (A-02 already BUSY from an abandoned run) | Ask Ibad to re-seed, or complete the leftover request. Plan says: abandoned run → re-seed before next attempt. |
| Phone works, dispatcher dead | Queue empty, “Reconnecting” | Ahmed still on localhost, or socket blocked | Swap his URL to Render; confirm `join:dispatch`. |
| Queue works, map blank | Row appears, no markers | Maps key / OSM not wired | Ahmed’s problem. Queue still proves the slice if markers don’t. |
| Assigned then never completes | Stuck at arrived, retry message | PATCH failed | Retry complete on the phone. If A-02 stays BUSY, seed is now dirty. |
| Two phones / two taps | Extra BUSY units | Two POSTs | Stop. Re-seed. One phone for the run. |

**Handoffs**
- Phone → Render: `POST /api/v1/emergency-requests` then `PATCH .../complete`. Timeout 45s. On timeout: user retry, no auto-retry (second POST would burn another ambulance).
- Render → phone: HTTP body for assignment (socket `request.assigned` is usually missed because you join the room after POST). Later events only if you stay in the room.
- Render → dispatcher: `queue.new` and `ambulance.updated` on room `dispatch`. If Ahmed never joined that room, he gets nothing even if POST succeeded.
- You → Ahmed: “tapping now.” He watches Live + queue. If his status never goes Live, stop before you tap.

**Cleanup:** a finished run must leave A-02 `AVAILABLE` again. Check `/api/v1/ambulances` after complete. If you kill the app mid-flow, do not start the next run until seed is reset.

### Docs half of Day 3 (cannot skip)

2. Screenshot dispatcher: same request in the queue + switch sentence.
3. Screenshot ambulances after complete (A-02 AVAILABLE).

Needs from you and Ahmed: those two screens at the same moment. Needs from Ibad: only if seed/Render breaks and he has to reset.

**You, before tomorrow if you want:** wake Render, `flutter run`, one solo phone pass against Render so tomorrow isn’t the first time that URL is used. That is rehearsal for Day 3, not Day 3 itself.

**Tomorrow, in person:** one coordinated run. You tap, Ahmed watches, Ibad is on the hook if `/health` or seed is wrong. Fix what that run breaks. Then screenshots.

**Not Day 3:** APK, GitHub Pages, demo script, freeze, three-in-a-row rehearsal. That’s Day 4.

Day 3 is done when one shared run has shown the switch on **both** screens and you have pictures plus a non-empty issue list. Until tomorrow, it is not done.

The reply recorded:

Keep the demo as it is. The 15-second “arrived → free” loop is a lie about hospitals, but it is the lie that lets you run the switch three times in a row. Do not put a hospital leg, a driver app, or a dispatcher “mark served” into the slice you already showed working.

The group chat is arguing two different buttons as if they were one.

**Dispatch served:** did a human actually send that unit from the bay? That is Sir’s level 2. Ahmed’s highlight / mark-done is this.

**Unit available:** is that ambulance free to take the next job? That is Ibad’s “driver declares free,” and your first-aid vs hospital split. Right now you fire this when the fake GPS hits the house.

If you use Ahmed’s “done” to free the vehicle, you free it while it is still driving to the patient. That is worse than what you have now.

## Current demo

The phone timer hits arrived, PATCH complete, A-02 goes `AVAILABLE`. Fine for a 2-minute show. Wrong for a transport job. Leave it.

## Your split (first aid vs hospital)

This is the right product split for October. First aid at home: the job can end at the door. Hospital: the unit stays `BUSY` until drop-off (or until someone says it is free).

What I would not do: invent a second map geofence at “the hospital” for the demo. You do not have a real hospital coordinate in the seed, and Sir already said user interaction is easier to show than map magic.

MVP shape: request type is `first_aid` or `hospital`. Same auto-booking you have now. Complete rules differ. First aid can complete at scene. Hospital cannot.

## Ibad (driver marks free)

This is the honest signal for `AVAILABLE`. The person in the vehicle knows if they are still with a patient.

You have no driver app. Do not start one for a supervisor meeting. For MVP, a tiny “unit is free” control is enough. Dispatcher can own that until a driver login exists. Same button, different person later. You said both work; I would start on the dispatcher you already have, and give the driver the same action when that screen exists.

Do not auto-free on map arrival for hospital jobs. GPS will lie (traffic, underground bay, phone in the glove box). Sir’s “or we do it using map?” is a real option, just a worse one to demo.

## Ahmed (auto-book, dispatcher clears the highlight)

This matches Sir almost exactly, and it is not the free/busy question.

Keep booking automatic. Queue row lands, already assigned. Highlight = “this Dispatch Request has not been Served.” On-ground manager taps Served after they have actually sent the crew. That tap does **not** free the ambulance. It only says: a human confirmed the physical send.

That is the “physical on ground verifiability” Sir asked for. The system cannot see a crew leave a bay. A map cannot either unless you trust GPS more than I would in Karachi traffic.

The reliability argument you sent him (“system does it to reduce human error”) is half right. Auto-assign reduces “who is nearest?” mistakes. It does not verify that the van moved. Those are different errors.

question from ibad. use @.cursor/rules/humanizer.md to explain your answers. if you have any confusions, ask via the tool

The reply recorded:

Ibad is mixing two jobs. One is telling a crew where to go. The other is seeing where the van is. Neither needs a driver smartphone. A driver portal is just one way to do both, and you already dropped it.

## How the dispatcher talks to the ambulance (many requests at once)

The dashboard is for the person in the room. The crew never looks at it.

Each unit already has a name: A-01, A-02. That is the radio callsign. Two requests at once does not mean one loudspeaker dump. It means two addressed calls.

Request 1 assigned to A-02, pickup Street 12, cardiac. Dispatcher (or the person with the handset) says something like: “A-02, Street 12, DHA Phase 5, cardiac, one patient.” Request 2 assigned to A-04 gets its own call. Same as 1122 / Edhi already work.

Your auto-booking still helps. The system has already picked who is nearest and not busy. The dispatcher is not choosing from a pile under pressure. They are reading the row the computer just made: unit, address, type. If two rows light up, they handle them in order, or a second person takes the second handset. That is staffing, not an app.

What you do **not** do: SMS the driver’s personal phone as the official channel. That is the smartphone you said they may not have, on a number you do not control, in a language the system does not log.

If the unit is sitting in the bay, some centres still walk over with a slip. Radio still wins once they are rolling.

For October I would keep assignment automatic, keep Ahmed’s highlight until someone marks Served, and treat Served as “I have actually told that crew / they have left.” The computer cannot hear a radio.

## How you track several vans that are moving

Without something in the vehicle, you do not track movement. You track **status**, and you show a **last known place**. Pretending the marker slides across Karachi on a 15-second demo timer is fine for the show you already did. It is fake for “real data.”

**Radio only.** Crew calls in: leaving bay, at scene, transporting, at hospital, clear. Dispatcher taps those states. Map jumps: base → pickup → hospital → free. Between taps the dot sits still. Several ambulances is several rows, same radio, different callsigns. This is how a lot of real fleets still run. It is accurate in the sense that a human confirmed it. It is not a live GPS trail.

**Box in the van.** A GPS/GSM tracker on the battery or OBD, maybe two thousand to eight thousand rupees a unit, its own SIM. No smartphone, no app the driver has to learn, no “driver forgot to open the portal.” Backend gets lat/lng every 10-30 seconds. Socket already has `ambulance.updated`. You reuse that. Then Ahmed’s map can actually move, and Ibad’s “they are not a constant” is a real stream.

Map-only “we inferred they arrived because the dot is near the house” will lie. Tunnels, flyovers, a tracker left in a parked van, a phone in a glove box. Sir already pushed user interaction over map magic for the demo. I would not switch that for hospital clear / unit free. GPS for **where**. A tap (dispatcher, from the radio) for **available**.

## What I would pick for October

Do not build a driver portal.

Do radio + dispatcher status as the source of truth for the request (served, at scene, to hospital, clear). That answers Ibad’s first question and the free/busy question from last night.

Add vehicle trackers only if you want live dots on the dispatcher map. That is the only honest answer to his second question. Seed coordinates plus a timer will not survive “real data.”

If trackers slip past October, ship radio-only and say so. A still marker with a timestamp (“last report 2 min ago, at scene”) is respectable. A smoothly moving icon with no device in the van is not.

You can paste Ibad this:

The crew gets the job by radio, by callsign, one request per unit. The dashboard tells the dispatcher what to say. It does not talk to the driver. Movement on the map needs a tracker in the van or we only show last reported place and status. Unit free stays a human tap, not a geofence.

The user asked:

the radio and box methods are redundant.
do this: via google scholar, find 5 research papers that solve or address this issue, and give me their links and summary and what they propose to fix

The reply recorded:

Ibad’s two problems show up in EMS research as one hardware problem: the van needs a unit that can (a) tell the centre where it is, and (b) carry the job details, without a driver smartphone. The papers do not replace that with software on your laptop. They put GPS + cellular on the vehicle, then let the dispatcher see many units at once.

One note before the list. Radio and a GPS box are not two ways of doing the same job. Radio (or a GSM voice call) is how you **tell** A-02 the address. The box is how you **see** A-02 move. The papers that look like they “remove the redundancy” still keep both functions. They just run them through one GSM/GPRS module in the ambulance so you are not maintaining a radio net and a separate tracker.

Scholar search for each title: [scholar.google.com](https://scholar.google.com). Direct paper links below.

---

**1. Shirani and Sehhati (2019). Design and implementation of a customable automatic vehicle location system in ambulances and emergency vehicle systems.** *Journal of Medical Signals & Sensors.*

- Paper: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6743240/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6743240/)
- Scholar: [search this title](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Design+and+implementation+of+a+customable+automatic+vehicle+location+system+in+ambulances+Shirani)

They built AVL hardware around a SIM908 (GPS + GSM + GPRS in one pack) for Az-Zahra Hospital’s fleet. Coords go over TCP/IP to a C# server; the centre sees the path on a map.

Two versions. Simple: the van only pushes lat/lng; the centre watches. Advanced: the same module lets the driver receive calls and SMS, so job details and location share one box. That is the closest published answer to “no driver portal, still talk to the crew, still track several moving units.”

---

**2. Banshwar et al. (2021). An efficient approach for ambulance tracking system using GPS and GSM.** *Journal of Physics: Conference Series* 1854 012009.

- Paper: [https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1854/1/012009](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1854/1/012009)
- Scholar: [search this title](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=An+Efficient+Approach+for+Ambulance+Tracking+System+using+GPS+and+GSM+Banshwar)

Arduino + SKG13BL GPS + SIM900A GSM, mounted in the vehicle. The hospital/base does not need a live app in the cab. Someone at the centre texts `Ambulance Track`; the box replies with coordinates. An LCD on the unit is optional.

Fix: treat the ambulance as a thing you query by SMS, not a person who must open an app. Several vans means several SIMs / IDs. Weak on “push the pickup address to the driver”; it is mostly tracking, not dispatch text.

---

**3. Satyanarayana, Sarma, Sravan, Malini, Venkateswarlu (2012). GPS and GPRS based telemonitoring system for emergency patient transportation.** *Journal of Medical Engineering.*

- Paper: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4787302/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4787302/)
- Scholar: [search this title](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=GPS+and+GPRS+Based+Telemonitoring+System+for+Emergency+Patient+Transportation+Satyanarayana)

They start from the complaint Ibad is circling: voice, location, and patient data usually sit on separate radios/SIMs, which is expensive and annoying for technicians. One ARM9 box in the ambulance packs GPS, voice, vitals, a patient snapshot, and sends one GPRS packet to a central monitoring station. The dispatcher sees the van on a map and can guide it. Aimed at Indian EMRI-style 108 services.

Fix: one cellular pipe for “where is the van” and “talk to the crew.” No driver smartphone. Still hardware in the vehicle (~USD 4500 in their build, so not a cheap puck).

---

**4. Płaczek (2017). The in-town monitoring system for ambulance dispatch centre.** arXiv:1706.03699.

- Paper: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03699.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03699.pdf)
- Scholar: [search this title](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=THE+IN-TOWN+MONITORING+SYSTEM+FOR+AMBULANCE+DISPATCH+CENTRE+Placzek)

Dispatch-centre design for several ambulances in a city. GPS + GIS for nearest free unit and route. Roadside cameras as a second way to see that a van is actually in that traffic, not only that a tracker says so. Mentions radio/GSM as part of the stack, not instead of GPS.

Fix for “multiple moving ambulances that are not a constant”: live GPS into the dispatch board, plus camera confirmation. Closest to Ibad’s second question. Does not remove a device from the van.

---

**5. Dimopoulou (2006). Implementation of an advanced spatial technological system for emergency situations.** FIG Commission 2, Budapest.

- Paper: [https://fig.net/resources/proceedings/2006/budapest_2006_comm2/papers/ts07_04_dimopoulou.pdf](https://fig.net/resources/proceedings/2006/budapest_2006_comm2/papers/ts07_04_dimopoulou.pdf)
- Scholar: [search this title](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Implementation+of+an+Advanced+Spatial+Technological+System+for+Emergency+Situations+Dimopoulou)

Field trial in Patras: each emergency vehicle had GPS + GPRS. Positions hit a trauma/dispatch centre and showed as updating lights on a city map. GIS picked routes. GSM carried telemedicine the other way. Three months with the National Centre for Emergency Response. They report shorter transfer times.

Fix: fleet map from vehicle-mounted GPS, computer routing so the centre is not reading addresses off a whiteboard when several calls hit at once. Crew still has in-vehicle kit; they trained people on it. Again, not a phone in the driver’s pocket.

---

**What this means for you**

None of these five solve Ibad’s problem with “dashboard only, nothing in the van.” The published fix is: a GPS/GSM unit **in the ambulance** (sometimes with voice on the same SIM), a server, a dispatcher map that can show many IDs at once. Job details go as SMS/call through that module, or by radio if you keep radio as backup.

If you drop both radio and the box, the literature does not offer a third method. You are back to shouting across a bay.

For October, the paper that maps onto Madad+ with the least new fiction is Shirani’s simple AVL (track only, reuse your `ambulance.updated` socket) plus SMS or a GSM call on that same module for the address. Satyanarayana is the citation if Sir asks why voice and tracking should share one device instead of two.

The user asked:

the radio and box methods are redundant.
do this: via google scholar, find 5 research papers that solve or address this issue, and give me their links and summary and what they propose to fix also we do not want to do any hardware stuff

The reply recorded:

One limit first, because the papers will look like they “solve tracking” if you skim the titles.

None of this literature replaces a radio or a GPS box as a **sensor**. They assume the control room already knows each job (address, type, assigned unit) and each unit’s **status plus origin/destination**. What they add is software: which unit to send when several calls overlap, and where to **draw** a moving van from a travel-time model. That is the no-new-hardware answer. It is an estimate, not a live ping.

## 1. Andersson and Värbrand (2007)

**Decision support tools for ambulance dispatch and relocation.** *Journal of the Operational Research Society*, 58, 195-201.

- [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Decision+support+tools+for+ambulance+dispatch+and+relocation+Andersson+V%C3%A4rbrand)
- [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1057/palgrave.jors.2602174)
- [Open postprint (PDF)](https://scispace.com/pdf/decision-support-tools-for-ambulance-dispatch-and-relocation-t1z5ytrp3u.pdf)

Built with SOS Alarm (Sweden 112). The problem they name is yours: the dispatcher must pick a unit **and** keep the city coverable while several calls are in play. Closest-available is not always right; sending A now can leave a hot district empty.

**What they propose:** a PC program (they say no special hardware). A “preparedness” score per zone. Auto-dispatch that can skip the nearest unit if that would wreck coverage. Dynamic relocation suggestions so idle units fill holes. Dispatcher still confirms. GIS shows the picture.

For you: keep auto-assign, but score “what happens to the rest of DHA if we take A-02” instead of distance only.

## 2. Schmid (2012)

**Solving the dynamic ambulance relocation and dispatching problem using approximate dynamic programming.** *European Journal of Operational Research*, 219(3), 611-621.

- [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Schmid+dynamic+ambulance+relocation+dispatching+approximate+dynamic+programming)
- [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2011.10.043)
- [Open PDF](https://prolog.univie.ac.at/research/publications/downloads/Sch_2012_465.pdf)

Vienna call data. Two software decisions on every event: who goes to this call, and where that unit waits after the job. Travel times and call volume change by hour. Closest-idle plus return-to-base is the baseline they beat.

**What they propose:** approximate dynamic programming. Learn a policy that sometimes does **not** send the nearest ambulance, then relocates the free unit to a better waiting point. About 13% shorter mean response in their tests (4.60 to 4.01 min).

For you: Ibad’s “many requests at once” is this. The queue is not first-come closest. The algorithm looks at current busy set and time of day.

## 3. Nasrollahzadeh, Khademi, and Mayorga (2018)

**Real-time ambulance dispatching and relocation.** *Manufacturing & Service Operations Management*.

- [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Real-Time+Ambulance+Dispatching+and+Relocation+Nasrollahzadeh)
- [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2017.0649)

Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. Same pile-up: a new call while units are already out. Closest-now can be worse than waiting 3 minutes for a unit about to clear nearby.

**What they propose:** ADP again, with a wider action set: send any idle unit, **or queue the call**, and optionally move an idle unit into the hole left by the one you just sent. They also write each ambulance as `(status, origin, destination, time movement started)`. Position on the map is computed from that, not from a tracker.

That last bit is the software-only “tracking” model. Marker slides along the planned trip. Wrong if the van is stuck in traffic. Good enough for a dispatcher picture without buying boxes.

Their policy cut high-priority late calls by about 30% vs the best static layout they tested.

## 4. Reuter-Oppermann, Morana, and Hottum (2017)

**Towards designing an assistant for semi-automatic EMS dispatching.** HICSS 2017.

- [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Towards+Designing+an+Assistant+for+Semi-Automatic+EMS+Dispatching+Reuter-Oppermann)
- [Open paper](http://hdl.handle.net/10125/41588)

They start from the same room you have: one dispatcher, many incidents, still mostly manual, stressed, does not trust a black-box assigner. No driver app in the design.

**What they propose:** a software assistant on the CAD screen. Pick an algorithm by context (life-threatening vs scheduled transport). Show **why** this unit (closest, coverage, wait). Dispatcher accepts or overrides. Explanations exist so they do not ignore the suggestion when two rows light up.

This is Ahmed’s portal, with a brain. Auto-book stays. The human tap is Sir’s “served,” except here the tap is “I accept this recommendation / I have actually sent them.”

## 5. Guigues, Kraiselburd, Montecinos, Toriello, and Vargas (2024)

**Management and visualization tools for emergency medical services.** arXiv:2409.09154. Companion algorithms: [arxiv:2409.09158](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09158).

- [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Management+and+Visualization+Tools+for+Emergency+Medical+Services+Guigues)
- [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09154)
- [HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09154)

Rio de Janeiro EMS data. Open map tool: calls, hospitals, **animated** fleets, several dispatch rules (closest-available, myopic, two greedy heuristics that keep a queue of overlapping calls).

**What they propose:** do not ping the van. Interpolate. `travelTime(A, B, t0)` plus `positionBetweenOriginDestination(...)` every few seconds along the street graph. Busy units have a trip type (to scene, to hospital, back to base). A unit can be reassigned **while still driving**. Queue is ordered by penalized wait, not only by who shouted first.

That is the cleanest published match to “track many moving ambulances with no driver portal and no extra hardware.” It is a predicted path from the assignment you already stored.

Live demo of their tool: [samu.vincentguigues.com](http://samu.vincentguigues.com).

## What this means for Madad+

Ibad asked two questions. Papers 1-4 answer the first: concurrent requests are a **policy** problem. Software picks (or queues) a unit; the dispatcher’s screen is the place that information lives. Getting it into the cab still needs whatever channel the centre already uses. These papers do not invent a new one, and you said you do not want new hardware.

Paper 3 and 5 answer the second **in software**: store origin, destination, start time, status. Move the Leaflet marker along the OSM route. Several vans are several such trips. When the dispatcher marks served / at scene / to hospital / free, you recompute the path. No box. No driver phone.

Do not tell Sir this is real GPS. Tell him it is estimated position from the dispatch record, which is what this literature actually does.

The user asked:

the radio and box methods are redundant. we dont want to do anything hardware related.

The reply recorded:

Then they are not redundant with each other. They are both **outside Madad+**. The station already has a way to talk to a crew. You are not building it, buying trackers, or wiring radios.

Software-only, for real data, looks like this.

**Telling the ambulance.** Auto-assign still picks A-02. The dispatcher screen shows unit, address, type. A person in the room tells that crew however they already do (shout across the bay, phone, radio they already own). Multiple requests = multiple rows, each with a callsign. Your app’s job is to not mix those rows up. It does not deliver the message into the van.

**Tracking movement.** You cannot. There is no device to ask. Drop “live moving ambulances” as a product claim.

What you *can* track is the **job**: queued, assigned, served (dispatcher confirms they have actually sent someone), at scene, to hospital, clear. Each tap is the dispatcher typing in what they were just told. The map marker sits at last known place (base, then pickup, then hospital if someone bothers to set it). Several units = several rows in that state. Not several GPS trails.

Unit free stays a tap, not a geofence. Same as Sir wanted, and it needs no hardware.

So for Ibad: we do not track moving vans in software without something in the van. We track requests and which unit is busy. Live dots were demo sugar. October should not promise them.

The user asked:

futher questions:
1. do ambulances have a certain standpoint or can they just stop anywhere?
2. do ambulances refill their supplies? if so, how frequently
3. how does an ambulance dispatcher system work?

for all 3, assume we're talking about karachi

The reply recorded:

Karachi does not run one ambulance system. Edhi and Chhipa move most patients. Aman (now largely folded into Sindh’s 1122 / [SIEHS](https://www.siehs.org/2025/06/free-ambulance-service-in-sindh/)) is the one that looks like a textbook dispatch centre. What follows is that split, not a single city SOP.

## 1. Standpoint or stop anywhere?

They are posted. They are not free-roaming taxis that wait in a random gali until a job appears.

A 2012 survey of Karachi EMS in *Annals of Emergency Medicine* is still the clearest public description: [Edhi vans sit at high-traffic accident intersections](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2012.06.320), run from a scatter of centres. Aman posted vans in catchment areas around stations. Aman’s own slides called those posts **key points**: after a drop-off the unit goes back to a key point for the next call, not “wherever the driver feels like parking.” They talked about [9 stations and ~90 key points](https://www.scri.edu.sg/files/PAROS%20Presentations/17%20April%202012:%20Dubai,%20United%20A/4_PAROS_meeting_junaid_razzak.pdf) covering the city. Later Aman briefings used zones and ~80 locations with a 10-minute target.

SIEHS still says Karachi dispatch is GPS-nearest-available, not one depot on I.I. Chundrigar sending every van across town.

So: a van *can* stop anywhere to pick someone up. That is the job. Idle vans wait at known posts (centre, chowk, hospital bay, key point). Hospital-owned vans often live at that hospital. Your DHA Phase 5 seed dots are closer to key points than to “stop anywhere.”

If a driver idles in a random side street, control cannot send the next job by neighbourhood knowledge, and traffic police will not love it either.

## 2. Do they refill? How often?

Yes, if they used anything. There is no public Karachi number like “every 3 calls” or “every 4 hours.”

Formal EMS (WHO-style, and what Aman/SIEHS aim at): start-of-shift checklist, then replace what you opened or contaminated **after that patient**, usually when you are back at the station or key point. Oxygen, gloves, dressings, drugs if it is an ALS van. Deep clean is separate (soiled job, or a slower cycle).

What actually happens on a lot of Edhi/Chhipa vans is thinner. Those fleets are mostly **transport**: stretcher, oxygen if you are lucky, first aid. A comparison study of Karachi services scored Edhi and Chhipa at **0%** on the infection-control and medicine subset; Aman was much higher but a smaller share of trips ([CIBGP](https://cibgp.com/index.php/1323-6903/article/view/2001)). So “restock after every run” is the rule on paper for a clinical ambulance. It is not what most Karachi volume looks like.

Punjab 1122 audits have also found expired stock and weak inventory. Sindh 1122 is newer and better equipped on paper; I would not assume every Karachi 1122 van is restocked to protocol every time.

For Madad+: you do not need a restock clock in the demo. If you model it later, restock is a **station event** after complete, not something that happens at the patient’s door. First aid at home might use almost nothing. A trauma run can empty a bag in one trip.

## 3. How does dispatch work here?

Someone calls a number: Edhi **115**, Chhipa **1020**, Aman **1101**, 1122 **1122** ([Commissioner Karachi list](https://commissionerkarachi.gos.pk/emergency-services)).

**Edhi-style (most of the city).** High volume, landmarks not pin drops, control talks to the van on a phone. Nearest unit is whoever the operator thinks is closest and free. A 2012 snapshot: ~1100 calls/day, ~10 minutes call-to-dispatch, ~60 minutes transport, delays blamed on traffic and nobody giving way to sirens. Half of Edhi’s work in that period was home-to-hospital, not roadside crashes.

**Aman / SIEHS-style.** A command room. One person takes the call with a script (they used ProQA / MPDS: how old, breathing, chest pain, etc.) and a dispatch code. Another person (wireless operator) picks a unit and tells the crew. Historically they had trackers and maps; SIEHS still advertises GPS nearest-unit. Station gets a heads-up. Crew treats / loads, goes to hospital, then **back to the key point**. Aman also used to say the call-taker has ~90 seconds before they must be ready for the next caller, and dispatch can go out while someone is still on the line with the family.

That second model is what Sir described, just with Karachi names: system (or call-taker) creates a dispatch request; an on-ground dispatcher/wireless op actually sends a van and marks it gone.

You are not building 115. You are building a small version of that room: auto-pick the unit, show the row, a human confirms they have told the crew. The city already has phones and radios. Your software does not need to be those.

Numbers in old papers (400 Edhi vans, 100 Aman, 6-10 minute Aman targets) are stale. The **pattern** has not changed: posted vans, a room that assigns, then a hospital, then back to a post.

The user asked:

futher questions:
1. do ambulances have a certain standpoint or can they just stop anywhere?
2. do ambulances refill their supplies? if so, how frequently
3. how does an ambulance dispatcher system work?

for all 3, assume we're talking about karachi. use @.cursor/rules/humanizer.md to make it simple to understand

The reply recorded:

Karachi does not run one ambulance system. Edhi and Chhipa do most of the rides. They are mostly “get the patient to a hospital.” Aman (now under [SIEHS / Sindh 1122](https://www.siehs.org/2026/05/from-call-to-care-what-happens-when-you-call-1122-for-an-ambulance/)) is the smaller, more “EMS” layer: triage software, stations, a control room. Your questions have different answers depending on which one you mean.

## 1. Standpoint or stop anywhere?

They are supposed to wait at known spots. Not anywhere the driver feels like.

A 2012 survey of Karachi EMS put it plainly: [Edhi posts vans at high-accident intersections](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2012.06.320), out of a scatter of small stations. Aman put vans in catchment areas around planned stations. An older Aman briefing said the city was covered with a handful of stations plus about 90 “key points,” and after a call the van goes **back to a key point** for the next job, not home, not a random paan shop.

That is why you see an Edhi van sitting at a busy chowk, under a flyover, or outside a hospital gate. That is a standpoint. The point is to sit where crashes and calls already cluster, so the next one is close.

Can they stop anywhere in practice? A crew can get flagged down on Shahrah-e-Faisal. That happens. It is not the official model, and the control room may not even know that van is busy until someone calls it in.

For Madad+: seed units at fixed DHA points is closer to Aman/key-point staging than to “drive around until someone waves.” After a job, the honest software move is: back to standpoint, then `AVAILABLE`. Not “free at the patient’s door” unless it was first aid and they never left the street.

## 2. Do they refill supplies? How often?

Yes, if they carry anything worth refilling. A lot of Karachi vans barely do.

Edhi’s fleet in that same survey was basic first aid. Aman had a subset with defibrillators, airway kit, drugs. A later Karachi paper rated Edhi/Chhipa at **0%** on medicine and infection-control checks. So “how often do they restock” for the big charities is often: oxygen when the cylinder is empty, bandages when the station has stock, not a tight checklist after every call.

Where it is done properly (Aman-type / textbook EMS):

- Anything used on this patient is replaced **before the van is marked free again**. Often a 1-for-1 swap at the hospital, or back at the station.
- Full inventory at the **start of the shift**.
- Oxygen is the one everyone understands: swap the bottle when it is low, not on a calendar.
- Drugs also expire. That is a monthly check, not a per-call thing.

There is no public Karachi rule that says “every 4 hours.” Frequency is **after each job that used stock**, plus a shift check. If the next call comes in before they have restocked, a proper control room keeps them off the “available” list, or sends them anyway and logs that they are short. That is the same `AVAILABLE` vs `BUSY` problem you already have, just for supplies instead of location.

For your app, you do not need a supply module for October. If you ever do: “not free until restocked” is a dispatcher tap, same as unit free. No hardware.

## 3. How does dispatch work in Karachi?

Someone calls (115, 1021, 1122, or a local number). A person in a room writes down where and what. Then they pick a van.

**Edhi-style:** lots of calls, landmark directions (“near Dolmen, after the signal”), phone to the crew. Mean call-to-dispatch was about 10 minutes in that 2012 snapshot. No fancy acuity software. The van is whoever is nearest *and answering*.

**Aman / SIEHS-style:** call taker runs a script (they use ProQA, the same family of questions as 911). A dispatch code comes out. Someone in the control room finds an appropriate ambulance, sends it, and the caller can stay on the line for CPR / bleeding instructions while the van is already rolling. Aman divided Karachi into zones and a pile of wait-locations so a van could reach in under ~10 minutes on paper. They also used vehicle tracking in the control room. That is *their* hardware, not yours.

After pickup: hospital, then back to the key point. The control room’s job in the middle is: this unit is busy, this one is free, this call is still waiting. When many calls hit at once, it is still one row per van, talked to by callsign. The computer (when they have one) suggests who is closest. A human still has to actually send them.

That is the two-level thing Sir described, in real clothes: the system (or the call taker) creates a request, the person on the floor makes the van move.

What this means for you: a standpoint list, auto-assign from whoever is free at those points, dispatcher marks served / free. Live moving dots and radio gear are what Aman bolted on top. You already decided not to build that.
